subject: Biology
title: Plant Life Cycles
description: A tiny lesson with a big payoff: Plant Life Cycles.

hook.text: Some plants live one season and die. Others survive for thousands of years. The strategies differ.

buildup.text: Annuals like wheat complete their life cycle in one year—germinate, flower, seed, die.

discovery.text: Perennials like oak trees live for decades, flowering and seeding many times.

twist.text: Bristlecone pines in California are over 5,000 years old—the oldest known individual organisms.

climax.text: Biennials take two years: grow vegetatively the first, reproduce the second, then die.

punchline.text: One year, two years, or five thousand. Plants play the long game.

quiz.question: How old are the oldest bristlecone pines?

details.summary: Plants alternate between a diploid sporophyte generation that produces spores and a haploid gametophyte generation that produces gametes. In flowering plants the sporophyte dominates while the gametophyte is reduced to pollen grains and embryo sacs hidden within flowers.
details.whyItMatters: Alternation of generations is a fundamental concept in plant biology that distinguishes plant reproduction from animal reproduction. Understanding it explains everything from moss life cycles to why flowers produce pollen and embryo sacs.
takeaways: All plants alternate between sporophyte and gametophyte generations
In mosses the gametophyte dominates; in flowering plants the sporophyte dominates
Pollen grains are the male gametophyte generation of flowering plants

faq.question: What is alternation of generations?
faq.answer: Plants cycle between a diploid sporophyte that produces haploid spores by meiosis and a haploid gametophyte that produces gametes by mitosis. When gametes fuse, they create a new diploid sporophyte. Animals have nothing equivalent to this two-stage life cycle.

faq.question: Why did the sporophyte become dominant in land plants?
faq.answer: Being diploid provides backup copies of genes, buffering against harmful mutations. Larger sporophyte bodies better resist desiccation and UV radiation on land. Ferns, conifers, and flowering plants progressively reduced gametophyte size while expanding sporophyte complexity.
